claim: Comparing two analogous cases and stating what they share produces more unaided transfer than one case. Gick & Holyoak 45% vs 21% (N=98); Catrambone & Holyoak 47% vs 16% (n=19 each); Gentner 2003 48% vs 19% (N=128); meta-analysis d=.50 over 57 experiments.
agent_test: At equal tokens: give the agent two solved cases of one class with a 'list what they share' step versus one case plus an unrelated case; test on a new instance of the class.

claim: Even with comparison, most learners do not transfer unaided in most lab conditions (about 40 to 48%), though comparison alone reached 70% in one live negotiation experiment and guided scaffolding (definition, diagrams, guiding questions) reached 90%. Transfer is real but partial.
agent_test: Report transfer rate per condition; do not assume a derived schema will be used.
audit_note: Gentner Exp 3 comparison alone (no heavy scaffolding) reached 70% unaided, contradicting "only heavy scaffolding reaches 70 to 90%"; sources are two labs.
claim_before_audit: Even with comparison, most learners do not transfer unaided in most lab conditions (40 to 48%); only heavy scaffolding reaches 70 to 90%. Transfer is real but partial.

claim: Studying cases separately gives little or no gain over no training, but this is contested: Loewenstein 2003 saw 22% vs 23% baseline, while Gentner 2003 Exp 3 saw 55% vs 37%.
agent_test: Arm with N cases shown one by one with a per-case summary, versus no cases, versus joint comparison.

claim: A stated principle added to a single analog adds nothing (32% vs 29% pre-hint), but added to a pair of analogs it raises noticing (62% vs 40%) and total solution (82% vs 67%). Seen in one paper; one student replication (Boyce et al. 2023, FORRT atlas) is marked successful and says the statement helped transfer from a pair of analogs, but gives no numbers. Alfieri's moderator says principles given after comparison beat principles given before.
agent_test: Pair of cases with and without an explicit principle line, and principle before vs after the comparison.

claim: Quality of the written schema predicts transfer (good schema 91% pre-hint vs poor 30%; principle quality in negotiation 88% vs 45%), but the link is correlational, small-sample and weak in Catrambone totals (67% vs 71%). Case-by-case advice quality did not predict behaviour.
agent_test: Score each induced rule on held-out instances (G3); check whether rule quality predicts later solve rate in our runs.

claim: Similar versus dissimilar pair of analogs makes no reliable difference to transfer (39% vs 52% pre-hint, not significant); dissimilar trended better. The claim that varied examples help rests on a trend.
agent_test: Choose the pair of cases by surface dissimilarity vs similarity at equal tokens.

claim: Unaided transfer vanishes after a 30-minute delay or a context change (no condition above the 10% base rate). It is partly rescued by directive comparison questions, a third example and target wording that matches the schema (74% unaided in the 1-week condition vs 7% and 23% earlier). The three changes were confounded.
agent_test: Separate the stored rule from its cue: test retrieval of a stored rule on a differently worded instance, with and without a rewording step.

claim: More guided comparison gives more transfer: definition plus diagrams plus questions 90% vs bare comparison 70% vs separate 55% vs baseline 37%; directive questions raised good schemas from 26% to 86%.
agent_test: Compare a bare 'find common structure' prompt with a structured form (fields: goal, constraint, mechanism, what is irrelevant).

claim: Case-comparison meta-analysis: d=.50 (95% CI .44 to .56), 57 experiments, 336 tests. Reliable moderators: comparison objective (find similarities best), principle presentation (after better), content, lag (immediate better). An earlier conference abstract gave d=.60. Abstract only read.
agent_test: Use 'find similarities' as the objective, not 'list differences', in the induction step.

claim: Step-back prompting gives large gains on weaker or mid models where the task needs principle recall (PaLM-2L Physics 66.4 to 73.2, Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8, TimeQA 41.5 to 66.0), but little on a strong model over CoT (GPT-4 Physics +1.6, Chemistry +0.3, within SD) and none on StrategyQA or GSM8K.
agent_test: Step-back versus plain short reasoning at equal tokens on our class mix; expect gains only where the plain pass rate is low and principle recall matters.

claim: Abstraction is rarely the failing step. After abstraction, over 90% of step-back errors are in reasoning (MMLU Physics); Self-Discover finds 87.5% of structures correct, with 74.7% of failures in computation.
agent_test: Do not spend tokens validating the abstract step; spend them on checked execution of the step (S4, G3).

claim: Step-back is not free: it fixes 20.5% of baseline physics errors but introduces 11.9% new ones (TimeQA: 39.9% fixed, 5.6% new). The net gain hides regressions.
agent_test: Run both arms and keep the plain answer as a candidate; select by check, not by defaulting to the abstracted answer.

claim: Stores of reusable abstractions built from past solved tasks raise accuracy on same-family tasks: Buffer of Thoughts (Game of 24 82.4 vs ToT 74.0; Checkmate-in-One 86.4 vs 57.2 meta-prompting), AWM (+12.0 WebArena), ReasoningBank (+4.6 to +8.3 WebArena over no memory), ExpeL. The store only grows in value if a manager updates it. Benchmarks are the authors' own and in-family.
agent_test: Task stream from one class: memory off vs on at equal tokens, with a held-out different class to detect leakage.

claim: Workflow memory gain is partly reuse of validated routines and partly abstraction. Rule-built workflows matched model-written ones on WebArena (35.6 vs 35.5 success), but model-written ones were better on Mind2Web (task success 4.8 vs 2.0, step success 45.1 vs 43.4). Whole-example retrieval was worse than both. See K31 for the wider ladder.
agent_test: Compare code-built versus model-built reusable routines at equal tokens.

claim: Self-generated analogs help large models by about 4 points on average (GSM8K 75.0 to 77.8, MATH 33.0 to 37.3 with GPT-3.5), fail on small models, and K=1 is worst (76.1 vs about 77.5 GSM8K) while K=3 to 5 is stable. The effect is small.
agent_test: Generate K=3 own examples versus none versus a retrieved example, at equal tokens, on a mid-size model.

claim: Abstraction-of-Thought: the AoT format beats CoT format when fine-tuned (BBH 10k samples: 49.7 vs 46.5 Llama-3-8B), and prompting alone adds +15.1 points in 3-shot BBH. AoT responses use about 80% more tokens and mix in code; the equal-token advantage is unmeasured. The headline needs training.
agent_test: Only the prompting form is usable; run abstract-plan-then-concrete versus CoT at equal tokens.

claim: LLM analogy success is brittle off the training distribution: GPT models fall sharply on counterfactual letter-string and shifted digit-matrix variants while humans do not (digit matrix GPT-3.5 0.813 to 0.480 with the blank moved). Webb 2023 found GPT-3 above the human mean on the original tasks, so this is contested and partly a contamination question. Newer reasoning models untested.
agent_test: Test any induced rule on a transformed, unfamiliar variant (renamed symbols, altered order) not seen in the cases.

claim: Given two candidate source stories, GPT-4 never picked the correct source unprompted (0 of 15 per target). With a hint it claimed the correct source every time but also the wrong one almost every time (precision 0.50 to 0.52, recall 1.00). Humans (N=46 per target) had precision 0.42 to 1.00 and recall 0.06 to 0.22 without a hint. The 29% and 50% figures in that paper belong to Gick and Holyoak 1983 Exp 2 (8/28 and 14/28), not to the authors' own data. Whether a forced causal-structure check (G3) fixes source choice was not tested by anyone.
agent_test: Check retrieved cases against causal structure before use; test with distractor cases.

claim: Hypothesis search (state rule candidates in words, implement as programs, run on examples) lifts GPT-4 on ARC from 23% (programs only) to 30% (LLM hypotheses) but is mixed elsewhere: list functions 71.3% vs 73.1% for plain two-shot.
agent_test: Rule candidates then code-run on examples versus code directly, at equal tokens, on ARC items.

claim: In list-function hypothesis search the generator is the bottleneck (46.4% correct), summarising drops 26% of correct hypotheses (12.1 points absolute), and 45.4% of programs that pass the shown examples fail ground truth (Parab et al.). In ARC (Wang et al.) summarising cost less (30 vs 33 tasks solved, about 9% relative) and a program that passed the shown examples almost always passed the test (one exception). So how weak 'passes the shown examples' is depends on the domain and the number of examples. The 26% figure belongs to the list-function study only.
agent_test: Never summarise the rule list before testing; test every raw candidate on a held-out input.

claim: Generalisation alone (SAGE-style merging of cases) gave no gain over storing raw examples (55% vs 55% in the sketch task); adding near-miss cases with different labels gave +7 points (62%, p<.01), and in the geospatial task ALIGN peaked at 77% vs 62% prototypes vs 53% examples. Tiny symbolic datasets.
agent_test: Store cases with near-miss contrast cases versus merged summaries versus raw cases at equal tokens.

claim: Comparison helps only when effortful and aligned: separate interpretation gave no benefit, joint interpretation with listed correspondences gave most insight; in two studies only 16 to 18% of separate-case learners linked the cases (vs 98 to 100% of comparers; 45% vs 90% in a third experiment); teams did no better than solo (32% vs 34%); one study found benefit only for learners who disliked maths. Several results come from one research group.
agent_test: Force an explicit alignment output (correspondence list) in the induction step; test against a free-form summary.
audit_note: Comparers linking the cases were 98% (Gentner Exp 2) and 100% (Loewenstein), not 88%; also Gentner Exp 3 found 45% of separate-case learners linked cases (vs 90%), so 16 to 18% holds only for Exp 2 and the teams study.
claim_before_audit: Comparison helps only when effortful and aligned: separate interpretation gave no benefit, joint interpretation with listed correspondences gave most insight; only 16 to 18% of separate-case learners linked the cases (vs 88 to 100% of comparers); teams did no better than solo (32% vs 34%); one study found benefit only for learners who disliked maths. Several results come from one research group.

claim: Self-Discover, a once-per-task-class reasoning structure composed from atomic modules, beats CoT: BBH +7 (PaLM 2-L) and +6 (GPT-4), T4D 69 vs 40 and 85 vs 52, MATH +8.5 (PaLM 2-L) but only +2 (GPT-4: 73 vs 71). It uses 10 to 40x fewer calls than self-consistency, and structures transfer between model families. Gains are largest on world-knowledge tasks and moderate on algorithmic ones (re-checked in the paper). Prompts are longer than CoT, so tokens are not equal.
agent_test: Per-class structure built once and reused versus per-instance reasoning; count setup tokens (G7).

claim: Extra reasoning prompts add little for reasoning-trained models. On GPQA Diamond a step-by-step instruction changed accuracy by +2.9 points (o3-mini), +3.1 (o4-mini) and -3.3 (Gemini Flash 2.5) while time rose 20 to 80%. DeepSeek reports that few-shot examples consistently degrade R1 (no numbers). Structured thinking styles help only large models on hard search tasks (StyleBench). No test exists of step-back, abstract-plan-first or Self-Discover on such a model.
agent_test: Run plain, terse-reasoning and each scaffold arm on our own held-out items with the current model; keep a scaffold step only if it beats the terse arm at equal tokens.

claim: Terse reasoning keeps most of the long chain-of-thought gain. GSM8K few-shot: GPT-4o 53.3 standard, 95.4 CoT, 91.1 Chain of Draft with about 40 tokens vs about 200 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet 64.6, 95.8, 91.4). Small models and zero-shot setups lose more. This is the nearest token-matched baseline available for gap 2.
agent_test: Use a terse-reasoning arm (about 40 tokens) as the fair control when a scaffold step costs extra tokens (G7).

claim: Comparing two unsolved problems at test time under an instruction to find one shared solution produced the convergence solution in 51% (Exp 1, N=293) and 40% (Exp 2, N=224), against 13% for one story plus one problem and 38% / 35% for comparing two solved stories. Two problems solved separately gave 16%, near baseline. The comparison must be directed.
agent_test: Operator candidate: write a sibling problem with the same structure, solve both under one shared-strategy instruction, compare with solving the target alone at equal tokens.

claim: Induction by comparing cases helps language models by a few points in some settings. LEAP (compare own wrong answers with right ones, write lessons): GPT-4 +7.5 on DROP and +3.3 on HotpotQA, under 1 point on GSM8K and MATH, and no gain for Llama-2-70B, which did not follow the lessons. Contrastive CoT (valid plus invalid chain): GSM8K 69.2 to 79.0 and AQuA +4.0 on GPT-3.5-Turbo, with doubled demonstration length. Reasoning-trained models are reported to lose with few-shot demonstrations. No study tests the full human recipe of two cases, forced alignment, derived rule and new instance.
agent_test: Arms: plain, one case, two cases with forced alignment, two cases plus wrong-versus-right contrast, self-made cases. Equal tokens, held-out instances with changed surface form.

claim: For models, a small number of cases is enough and more can hurt. Self-generated exemplars: K=1 is worst (GSM8K 76.1, MATH 34.8) and K=3 to 5 is stable (77.3 to 77.8; 37.0 to 37.3). For retrieved agent memory the best number was 1 and success fell to 44.4 with 4 experiences. Gains from K=1 to K=3 are 1 to 3 points. Whether the choice of pair (similar, different, near-miss) matters for models is still untested.
agent_test: Cap retrieved or generated cases at 2 or 3; test similar versus different versus near-miss pairs.

claim: A model-written rule is best checked by running it, not by judging its wording. In ARC, a program built from a written rule that passed all shown examples almost always passed the test. In list functions 45.4% of train-passing programs failed ground truth. Rule quality as judged by people predicted transfer for humans (91% vs 30%), but no study shows a model's own rule-quality score predicting its held-out success.
agent_test: Score each model-written rule on all shown examples and on a held-out instance; check whether a judge-rated quality score adds any prediction beyond that.

claim: Surface changes hurt models, but unevenly. GPT-4 on digit matrices: 0.813 original, 0.790 with symbols, 0.480 with the blank moved. Story analogies: 89% when the correct answer was first, 61% when second (GPT-4). Reasoning-trained o1-preview lost 17.5 points when one irrelevant clause was added to maths problems. No paper tests altered alphabets on current reasoning models or tests a rewording step as a rescue.
agent_test: Apply a stored rule to renamed or re-ordered instances with and without a restate-in-own-words step; use a relevance check for each clause.

claim: In agent memory, stored runnable routines and curated lessons beat raw reuse. WebArena (Gemini-2.5-flash): no memory 40.5, raw trajectories 42.1, workflows 44.1, distilled strategies 48.8. Dynamic Cheatsheet, GPT-4o on Game of 24: baseline 10, raw retrieval 6, curated code-based memory 93 to 99. PlugMem: structuring raw episodes 75.1 vs chunks 62.8 (LongMemEval). Part of each gain comes from other changes (stronger instructions, learning from failures, indexing), and all use the authors' own benchmarks.
agent_test: Three arms on a held-out task class: raw solved cases, code-built routines, model-written templates; same retrieval and tokens.

claim: Replication status is thin. The FORRT atlas lists one student replication of Gick and Holyoak (1983), Boyce et al. 2023, marked successful, with the verbal statement helping transfer from a pair of analogs; no sample size or effect size was found. A 2017 replication of Kurtz and Loewenstein could not be found or verified and should not be cited. The Alfieri 2013 moderator effect sizes remain unread because the full text is paywalled.
agent_test: None for the agent; this is a limit on how hard the human evidence should be leaned on.

claim: Design inference (untested): gate induction on a plain attempt. Skip it when the plain pass rate is high or the model is reasoning-trained (extra prompting gave about +3 or less, K24); use it when plain attempts fail or disagree and the task needs recall of a principle or a reusable method (step-back and Self-Discover gains were largest there, K10, K23). Step-back gave zero on StrategyQA and GSM8K, and LEAP gave under 1 point on strong-model math.
agent_test: Log plain pass rate and principle-recall need per item; compare gated against always-on induction at equal tokens.
